1:
The chapter opens on a king at the height of his prosperity and the worst decision of his life. Gill has the riches and honour still increasing, and makes them the reason Ahab sought friendship and affinity, to which Jehoshaphat agreed. Ellicott notes that the phrase is repeated word for word from the preceding chapter, and reads the degree of prosperity Judah had reached in the very fact that so powerful a monarch entered into so intimate a connection with her king. Henry divides the matter in two: Jehoshaphat growing greater, his wealth and honour increased upon him by piety and good management; and Jehoshaphat not growing wiser, or he would never have joined with that degenerate Israelite who had sold himself to work wickedness. What good could he get by a man so bad, Henry asks, or do to a man so obstinately wicked, an idolater and a persecutor?

The affinity was a marriage. Clarke states it plainly, that Jehoshaphat took Athaliah to be wife to his son Joram; Ellicott dates the match eight or nine years before the visit that follows, and the visit itself to the sixteenth or seventeenth year of the reign. Henry calls it the worst match that ever was made by any of the house of David, and wonders what Jehoshaphat could promise himself by it. Perhaps pride made it, as it does many a one: his religion forbade him to marry his son to any of the heathen princesses about him, and having riches and honour in abundance he thought it a disparagement to marry him to a subject, so a king's daughter it must be, and therefore Ahab's — little considering that Jezebel was her mother. Others, Henry allows, think it policy, a hope of uniting the kingdoms in his son, with Ahab flattering him that he would make him his heir when he intended no such thing.

Then came the feast and the league. Keil and Delitzsch set this account beside the fuller one in Kings and find them agreed except in the introduction: there it is noted that after three years without war between Aram and Israel Jehoshaphat came up in the third year, and that Ahab, having determined with his servants to snatch Ramoth in Gilead back from the Syrians, called on him to march; the chronicler exchanges that exact date, which means nothing apart from the earlier history, for a vague one. Gill reports two years from the Syriac and Arabic. Ellicott reads the royal hospitality as part of a deliberate plan to obtain Jehoshaphat's co-operation, and glosses the verb rendered persuaded as incited or pricked on, a word used especially of urging to evil. Henry says as much more bluntly: the entertainment was designed only to wheedle him into the expedition, and the kisses of an enemy are deceitful. He presses the irony of the request, that Ramoth and every city of Israel belonged of right to Jehoshaphat as heir of the house of David, so that with what face could Ahab ask help in recovering it for himself, whose own title was usurped and precarious? Yet Jehoshaphat, an easy man, yields: I am as thou art. Some men's kindnesses are dangerous, Henry concludes, as well as their society infectious.
4:
Jehoshaphat's first instinct was the right one. Henry remarks that this passage is almost word for word what stands in Kings, declines to repeat what was said there, and draws six reflections instead; the first is the duty of acknowledging God in all our ways and enquiring at his word, whatever we undertake, for Jehoshaphat was not willing to proceed until he had done it. The enquiry is made, Henry adds, by particular believing prayer, by an unbiased consultation of the scriptures and our own consciences, and by an observant regard to the hints of providence. Wesley gives that counsel back in almost the same words. Clarke sets the two kings against each other out of the Targum: Ahab consulted false prophets, but Jehoshaphat sought instruction from the presence of the Lord and prayed at the entering in of Samaria, and before these all the false prophets prophesied lies.

Henry's second and third reflections turn on the company Jehoshaphat was keeping. The danger of bad company reaches even good men: here, in complaisance to Ahab, he sits in his robes patiently hearing lies spoken in the name of the Lord, can scarcely find in his heart to give so much as a mild reproof to a king who hates a prophet of the Lord, and will neither rebuke the false prophet who abuses the faithful seer nor oppose the imprisonment that follows. Those who venture among the seats of the scornful, Henry says, cannot come off without a great deal of the guilt that attaches at least to the omission of their duty. The third is the unhappiness of a man surrounded by flatterers who cry peace and prophesy nothing but smooth things: so Ahab was cheated into his ruin, and justly, for he preferred those who humoured him to the one prophet who warned him. That counsel is not always best for us which is most pleasing to us.

Ellicott works through the wording. Where Kings has about four hundred prophets he finds the number given flatly, and where Kings says the Lord the chronicler says the true God; Ahab's question is put in the singular, shall I go, which is the more appropriate form. Ahab's complaint has been sharpened too, from he prophesieth not good unto me to he is not prophesying to me for good but all his days for evil, which extends the grievance over the man's whole career. The name Micaiah presupposes an older form meaning who is like Iahu, and Iahu is probably the oldest shape of the divine name; the father's name means he is full, or he filleth. When Jehoshaphat asks the king not to speak so, Ellicott hears him deprecating an omen. The two kings were sitting each on his throne, and the pronoun that makes their robes their own is missing from the Hebrew, so that Ellicott prefers the reading preserved in the Syriac, clothed in raiment spotted white and black; the void place where they sat is literally a threshingfloor, rendered open ground by the Greek, and he suspects the word is corrupt and grew out of the term for spotted, perhaps embroidered, an epithet of robes. The participle used of the court prophets at the throne also means mad or raving, while the plainer form at the horns of iron means simply were prophesying; the root is probably the Assyrian verb to call or proclaim, so that a prophet is a herald. In Micaiah's own first answer, go ye up and prosper, Ellicott finds the chronicler has substituted a reply stating definitely that the Syrians shall be delivered into the hands of the allied kings, and is reminded of the Delphic oracle, that if a certain king crossed the Halys a mighty empire would be overthrown.
15:
Ahab's adjuration, Ellicott observes, is the same demand the high priest would one day put to Christ. What follows is a vision of a leaderless army, the people scattered on the mountains as a flock of sheep and goats with no shepherd. The council scene that comes next the chronicler has abridged: in Kings the whole host of heaven stands by the throne on the right hand and on the left, here only on the right. Ellicott notes that the Greek translators read the opening word as a denial rather than a consequence, and that the odd dialogue form of the next verse, one saying thus and another saying thus, is certainly the right text.

Who the volunteer spirit was, the Targum thought it knew, and Clarke calls its answer a strange gloss. The spirit of Naboth of Jezreel came out from the abode of the righteous and stood before the Lord and said, I will deceive him; and when the Lord asked by what means, he answered, I will be a spirit of false prophecy in the mouth of his prophets; and the Lord said he might, but that although the power was given him it would not be lawful for him to sit among the righteous, since whoever speaks falsely can have no mansion there: go forth from me and do as thou hast said. Ellicott keeps closer to the words, rendering a spirit of falsehood rather than a lying spirit, and sets beside it the place in Ezekiel where God says of a deceived prophet that he himself deceived him, the verb there being the one rendered entice here.

Henry takes the permission as the point of the passage, in two reflections. One lying spirit, by divine permission, can make four hundred lying prophets and use them to deceive a king, so that the devil becomes a murderer by being a liar and destroys men by deceiving them; and there is justice in God giving up to strong delusions those who will not receive the love of the truth but rebel against it. Wesley repeats the first of these almost word for word, and the last of them too. Henry's closing reflection is the hard case of faithful ministers, whose lot it has often been to be hated and persecuted and ill-treated for being true to their God and just and kind to the souls of men: Micaiah, for discharging a good conscience, was buffeted, imprisoned and condemned to the bread and water of affliction, yet could appeal with assurance to the issue, as all may who are persecuted for their faithfulness, since the day will declare who was right and who wrong.

Two details of the sentence draw Ellicott's attention. Zedekiah is told not that he may see but that he is destined to see, on the day when he enters a chamber within a chamber to hide himself; and since nothing more of his history is recorded, Ewald justly infers that the original narrative held a good deal more than the extract now before us. The prison fare is in the Hebrew no genitive but an accusative: not bread of affliction but bread with stint, water with stint, the word meaning literally a squeezing, which the Vulgate turns into a little bread and a very little water and the Syriac into enough of each to keep life. At the last Micaiah turns from the kings to the crowd and makes the bystanders witnesses, and the words he uses, hearken ye, O peoples all, open the book of Micah. Hitzig thinks they were taken from there; Thenius argues instead that the section bears indubitable marks of historical truth and is probably an extract from the history of Jehoshaphat written by Jehu the son of Hanani.
28:
The two kings go up, and the first thing the chapter records of the battle is a disguise and a set of royal robes. Ellicott hears Ahab's words as a hurried exclamation, disguising myself and entering, and notes that where Kings has Ahab alone going into the fight this account has both of them go, with the Syriac, the Greek, the Vulgate, the Arabic and the Targum agreeing. The order to the Syrian captains names no number here, though Kings gives thirty-two, a detail belonging to an earlier war the chronicler has not noticed; the Syriac and Arabic supply it. When the captains close on Jehoshaphat the verb is better rendered came round against him than turned aside against him, the difference in the Hebrew turning on half a letter.

Henry reads a plot in the robes. He thinks it reasonable to suppose that Ahab, while professing friendship, was really aiming at Jehoshaphat's life, to take him off and so have the management of his successor, who was his own son-in-law; otherwise he would never have advised him to enter the battle in his royal raiment, which was only to make himself an easy mark. If that was the design, Henry says, it was as unprincipled a treachery as ever man was guilty of, and Ahab was justly taken in the pit he had dug for his friend. The enemy had an eye on the robes soon enough and attacked the unwary prince vigorously, who now, too late, would have wished himself in the habit of the poorest soldier.

What the cry meant is left open. Henry offers three readings: that Jehoshaphat called to his friends to relieve him, which Ahab took no care to do; or to his enemies, to let them know their mistake, that he was not the king of Israel; or perhaps to God for succour and deliverance, and to whom else should he cry? Wesley gives the same three in the same order, and adds that it was not in vain. Ellicott settles on the third. He points out that the Kings account ends at the cry, so the clause about the Lord helping him and inciting the captains away is evidently from the chronicler's own pen, and that the chronicler must therefore have taken the cry for a prayer, a sense the verb often bears. How God drove them off the next verse explains: the captains discovered their mistake and retired. That perfectly natural event the chronicler treats as providential, and rightly so, Ellicott adds, since Hebrew faith knows nothing of an order of the world that can be separated even in thought from the constant personal activity of God. Clarke lets the Targum say it shortest: Jehoshaphat cried, and the Word of the Lord brought him assistance. Henry draws the same conclusion in his own terms, that God has all men's hearts in his hand and turns them as he pleases, contrary to their own first intentions, so that many are moved unaccountably both to themselves and others, but an invisible power moves them.
33:
The arrow that killed Ahab was shot by a man not aiming at him, and the commentators linger over the phrase. Ellicott compares a similar expression elsewhere which Gesenius interprets as without thought of evil design; he calls the Greek rendering with good aim a bad guess, reports the Syriac innocently straight before him, and judges the explanation of Rashi best of all, that the archer did not know why he chose that particular man to shoot at. Clarke prefers the Targum, which supplies both a name and a motive. Naaman, captain of the host of the great king of Syria, drew a bow against him, that the prophecy of Elijah the Tishbite and of Micaiah the son of Imla might be fulfilled, and smote the king of Israel between the heart and the caul of the liver, through the place where the coat of mail is joined. Where the arrow went in nobody knows: Ellicott takes the joints of the harness for the breastplate, with the Syriac reading between the division of his mail, and dismisses both the Greek, in the midst of the lungs and breast, and the Vulgate, between the neck and shoulders, as mere guesses.

What Ahab did next both Clarke and Ellicott admire. Ellicott reads the Hebrew as the king continuing to hold himself up in the chariot, facing Aram, until the evening, and prefers it to the reading in Kings, which has him held up and dying at evening, because the sense here is that Ahab bravely bore up against the pain of his wound in order not to discourage his own side by retiring from the field. Clarke says as much at more length and calls it true personal courage and patriotism: Ahab knew that if his troops found he was mortally wounded they would give way at once, and that the slaughter in the pursuit would be great, so he held on until the close of day must end the fighting anyway, and when it did the Israelites found their king dead and left the field to their foes. Thus Israel had a great loss and the Syrians a great deliverance, Clarke says, where but for this accident the Syrians had probably been defeated.

Ellicott notices what the chronicler leaves out. The rest of the story in Kings, the return of the army and the washing of Ahab's chariot at the pool of Samaria, is omitted because Jehoshaphat had no part in it, and perhaps because the chronicler had a true perception of the real climax of this vivid story of the olden time. Henry finds that climax in the contrast of the two kings: wicked Ahab disguising himself, arming himself, as he thought securing himself, and slain all the same, for no art and no arms can save those whom God has appointed to ruin. What can hurt those whom God will protect, and what can shelter those whom God will destroy? Jehoshaphat is safe in his robes and Ahab killed in his armour, since the race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong. Wesley puts the same antithesis in two lines. Clarke closes with a caution he says the reader should never forget, that God is repeatedly represented in the Bible as doing what, in the course of his providence, he only permits to be done.
